title: 2025 in review: what changed for India's workers
author: Editorial Desk
summary: Seventy years of BMS, the ELI scheme, the Codes and a quieter but important change in scheme workers' talks.
body:
As the year closes, this post looks back at what mattered to India's workers in 2025. It draws on the earlier posts on this blog and, wherever a fact can be checked, on official or well-reported public sources. The year had a clear shape: long-standing ideas about wages, social security and employment moved from debate towards law, and the question for workers moved from "will it happen?" to "will it reach me?"

## January to April: asking before the Budget

The year began with the usual season of pre-Budget consultations. BMS asked the Government to notify the Labour Codes and to give recognition to scheme workers, such as Anganwadi, ASHA and mid-day meal workers, who deliver public services without the status of employees. The Union Budget of 1 February 2025 included one measure aimed at a new kind of worker: the Finance Minister announced identity cards and registration on the e-Shram portal for gig workers on online platforms, with health cover under the Pradhan Mantri Jan Arogya Yojana, expected to benefit nearly one crore workers. It was among the first steps that put platform workers on the Government's map.

In April, as recorded in an earlier post, BMS called at an international congress for the regulation of artificial intelligence so that new technology does not simply replace working people.

## May to July: Geneva, a job scheme and a milestone

In June, the 113th International Labour Conference met in Geneva, opening on 2 June. It adopted the ILO's first convention, with a recommendation, on protection against biological hazards at work, on 13 June. It also began the process of setting a standard on decent work in the platform economy. A majority voted to pursue a binding convention supported by a recommendation, with the discussion to conclude at the 2026 conference. For India, where millions work through delivery and ride-hailing apps, a global standard matters because it would set a benchmark for how such work is classified and protected.

On 1 July, the Union Cabinet approved the Employment Linked Incentive (ELI) scheme, with an outlay of Rs 99,446 crore. The Government said it aims to support more than 3.5 crore jobs over two years, including about 1.92 crore first-time employees, for jobs created between 1 August 2025 and 31 July 2027. A first-time employee registered with the EPFO can receive one month's EPF wage, up to Rs 15,000, in two instalments, after six and twelve months of service. Employers who add jobs also receive incentives. BMS welcomed the scheme with conditions, as an earlier post on this blog explains.

On 23 July, BMS completed seventy years. The organisation was founded on 23 July 1955 by Dattopant Thengadi. The concluding programme of the seventieth foundation year was held in New Delhi, with Union Labour Minister Mansukh Mandaviya as guest of honour, and RSS chief Dr Mohan Bhagwat addressing it. BMS leaders spoke of the large unorganised sector and of the need to manage technological change so that it benefits labour, and set their sights on the centenary.

## August to October: scheme workers and remembrance

In the months after, the national leadership of BMS met and asked for early implementation of the Wage and Social Security Codes; an earlier post on this blog records the 159th meeting of the Kendriya Karya Samiti. A delegation also met the Education Minister on the concerns of mid-day meal workers. The condition of scheme workers remained a live issue. In Parliament on 1 August 2025, the Government said that it had no proposal under consideration to raise the honorarium of Anganwadi workers and helpers, which stood at Rs 4,500 a month for workers at regular centres and Rs 2,250 for helpers, as last revised in October 2018. That is the background to the continued BMS demand for better honorarium and eventual recognition.

The season of Vishwakarma Jayanti and the remembrance of Thengadi Ji gave the organisation occasions to restate its view that the worker is a builder of the nation and not only a seller of labour.

## November: the Codes come into force

The biggest event of the year came on 21 November, when the Government brought all four Labour Codes into effect: the Code on Wages, the Industrial Relations Code, the Code on Social Security and the Occupational Safety, Health and Working Conditions Code. They consolidate 29 central labour laws. The Government's announcement listed appointment letters for all workers, minimum wages for all workers, a national floor wage, social security for gig and platform workers, a free annual health check-up for workers aged 40 and above, and gratuity after one year for fixed-term employees. It said that social security coverage had risen from about 19 per cent of the workforce in 2015 to over 64 per cent in 2025, which is the Government's own figure.

BMS responded in a particular way, and this is worth stating exactly. On the day, a delegation led by General Secretary Ravindra Himte met the Labour Minister and submitted a memorandum. It called the Code on Wages and the Code on Social Security historic and pro-worker, but said it strongly opposed certain provisions of the Industrial Relations Code and the OSH Code. It also asked for the Indian Labour Conference, not held since 2016, to be convened, and listed demands such as raising the EPF wage ceiling from Rs 15,000 to Rs 30,000, a minimum pension of Rs 7,500, and higher honoraria for scheme workers. A delegation of unorganised sector federations also met the Minister that month, as recorded in an earlier post.

## December: a divided landscape

In December, BMS raised the Air India Express question, with a press statement on 9 December asking the Civil Aviation Ministry to intervene on cabin crew grievances. On 16 December, sixteen central trade unions, including BMS, stated at a summit in New Delhi that they supported the four Codes and would work to spread awareness of them. Other central unions took the opposite view and called for protest, a division that carried into the new year.

December also saw a new law on rural employment: the Viksit Bharat guarantee law, which received the President's assent and replaced the MGNREGA framework, with a guarantee of 125 days of work. How it works in practice is a question for 2026.

## The thread that runs through the year

The thread is the movement of ideas into law, and the work that is left. A worker does not benefit from a Code until three things are in place: rules that are made and notified, schemes that are funded, and money that actually reaches the person. For the Codes, that means State rules, registration systems for unorganised and platform workers, and inspection that is aimed at compliance. For the ELI scheme, it means that jobs are created and the incentive is paid. For scheme workers, it means an honorarium that keeps pace with living costs.

## Looking ahead

Three things will be worth watching in 2026: the finalisation of rules under the Codes, the Union Budget on 1 February, and the ILO's second discussion on platform work. BMS has said that it will keep two tracks open, dialogue with the Government on what it supports and protest on what it opposes. Whether one agrees with every position or not, the year showed that a large union can welcome parts of a reform, resist other parts and keep asking for the same basic thing: that a worker's work be recognised, protected and paid for fairly.
